title: The Sunday Essay: In Defence of Freud
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon defends Freud not as a doctrine but as a diagnostician of the civilised self under strain. He opens with Maya, who sees a colleague labelled as lacking resilience and instead reads his brittleness as the product of a role stuffed with contradictory demands. The essay then sets out Freud's central insight that civilisation is a bargain that buys order at the price of restraint, which shows up as guilt, ambivalence and defence. He argues that mixed feeling is the normal condition of dependence on institutions and people, and that defences are how people stay functional inside contradictions they cannot openly resolve. The practical payoff for leaders is to locate distress in selves-in-roles-in-systems and ask what should change, which Maya demonstrates by redesigning the role rather than coaching the man.
points: Dismissing Freud as outdated misses his real subject, which is what social order costs the self.
Ambivalence toward the roles and institutions we depend on is normal, not a failure of character or resilience.
Defences such as bursts of intensity, flatness or perfectionism can be rational adaptations to contradictory role demands rather than personal fragility.

Resilience language privatises strain that is often structural, so leaders should ask whether the role needs redesign, the contradiction needs naming, or a culture of constant responsiveness needs interrupting.

Maya's intervention clarified what the colleague actually owned, cut performative reporting and made room for mixed feeling, leaving him less brittle without pretending the organisation had stopped producing strain.
quotes: Freud keeps alive a truth that modern psychologies make too small: people do not suffer in a vacuum. They suffer in history, in institutions, in moral orders, in systems of dependence, performance, attachment, and guilt.

The central mistake is to treat Freud as though he were mainly trying to do what contemporary psychology does, only less competently. That misses the point. He was not simply constructing a psychology of isolated individuals. He was trying to understand what it costs a person to become fit for social life.

But that order is not free. It depends on restraint. It requires people to govern themselves, inhibit impulses, manage aggression, defer gratification, internalise rules, and accept limits they did not choose.

Distress stops looking like a simple defect in the individual and starts looking like one of the ways social life is lived inwardly. The person suffers, yes. But the suffering is not generated by some sealed-off personal weakness alone. It is shaped by the difficult psychological work required to remain attached, productive, moral, legible, and acceptable within an organised world.
Ambivalence, in this sense, is not a glitch in otherwise healthy feeling. It is a normal consequence of living in dependence on imperfect people and demanding systems.

This is where the practical value lies. A better use of Freud does not end with interpretation. It makes it easier to ask what should change so that people do not have to defend so hard just to remain functional.

That, Maya realised, was why the usual language of resilience kept missing. It was treating the strain as though it lived inside the person alone. Much of what looked like fragility through that lens was actually defended adaptation to contradiction.
